id: qc-06
title: HHL linear systems
paper: Harrow, Hassidim & Lloyd, Quantum algorithm for linear systems of equations (arXiv Nov 2008; PRL 103, 150502, 2009)
link: https://arxiv.org/abs/0811.3171
type: Theory
cutoff: 2008-11-19
domain: qc
profile: advantage

## expected_verdict
Supported (conditional). The algorithm and its near-optimality (matrix inversion is BQP-complete) stand. An end-to-end exponential speedup for a classical problem holds only if four input/output conditions hold (Aaronson's caveats). A claim of fast classical-vector solving is unsupported. This matches our deprioritized-HHL rule.

## I0
Can a quantum algorithm prepare a solution state for sparse, well-conditioned linear systems efficiently?

## evidence
- Task as defined by the authors: given s-sparse N×N A with condition number κ and vector b, estimate x†Mx for x = A⁻¹b, not x itself (Abstract).
- Runtime: poly(log N, κ); scales as ~κ² log(N)/ε for additive error ε in |x⟩ (§I), with sparsity entering via Hamiltonian simulation; classical comparator stated as Õ(N√κ) (Abstract). Exponential advantage when κ and 1/ε are polylog(N).
- Optimality (§III): matrix inversion is BQP-complete; improving κ-dependence to κ^(1−δ) would let any quantum computation be sped up, so the runtime is nearly optimal.
- Requirements: efficient preparation of |b⟩ and efficient Hamiltonian simulation of e^(−iAt) (sparse A).
- Output: quantum state |x⟩; reading N entries costs ~N repetitions (§I).

## intake
- Scope: prepare |x⟩ ∝ A⁻¹|b⟩ and estimate an expectation value of x in time poly(log N, κ).
- Regime: sparse (or efficiently simulable) A; κ = polylog(N); b efficiently loadable; output = expectation value or sample.
- Assumptions: fast state preparation of b (qRAM or formula); efficient e^(−iAt); well-conditioned A; user needs only a global property of x.
- Falsifier (end-to-end claim): any of the four conditions failing for the target application, or a classical algorithm with matched access computing the same property in polylog(N).

## screen
- Must flag Aaronson's four caveats: (1) loading b; (2) applying e^(−iAt); (3) κ must be small; (4) output is |x⟩, not x.
- Must request: the full task cost including state preparation and readout.

## retrieval
- Pre-cutoff must-finds: sparse Hamiltonian simulation (Berry, Ahokas, Cleve & Sanders 2007; Aharonov & Ta-Shma); phase estimation (Cleve, Ekert, Macchiavello & Mosca); classical Krylov / conjugate-gradient solvers as the comparator.
- Current mode: Aaronson 2015, "Read the fine print": the four caveats; HHL is "not exactly an algorithm for solving a system of linear equations in logarithmic time". Related: Tang-style dequantization of low-rank variants.

## designer
- Account for the full pipeline: data load, Hamiltonian simulation, κ, readout. Compare (a) expectation-value output and (b) full-vector output separately against the best classical solver with matched access.

## champion
- Conjugate gradient / Krylov methods with preconditioning for (b); for (a), classical sampling-based estimators of x†Mx with ℓ2-sampling access when A is low-rank.

## panel
- Accept the algorithm; reject wording that implies fast classical solution vectors. Repair: state outputs and input assumptions explicitly.

## run
- Theory check of runtime and the BQP-completeness reduction. Optional toy: 4×4 system in simulation, verifying |x⟩ fidelity vs κ; this certifies nothing about scaling.

## verdict
- Label: Supported (conditional) for the algorithm; unsupported for an unconditional end-to-end speedup on classical data.
- Must say: exponential speedup only when all four conditions hold; the paper itself frames the task as estimating x†Mx.
- Must not say: HHL is wrong; or HHL gives exponential speedup for generic linear-system solving.

## audit
- Check: poly(log N, κ); BQP-completeness in §III; κ^(1−δ) statement; Aaronson's four caveats in order.

## variants
- Quantum-native inputs (b prepared by another quantum process) and limited-observable outputs, e.g. inside quantum simulation pipelines.
